books.section: America in an Era of Turmoil (1960-1975)

source: original; stimulus table compiled from the Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables, Table 1.3

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables, Table 1.3, and the Census Bureau, Statistical Abstract, Table 539.
stimulus.text:
Federal spending, 1950-1980 (Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables, Table 1.3; defense shares from the Census Bureau, Statistical Abstract, Table 539, using Office of Management and Budget figures):

| Fiscal year | Federal outlays as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) | Defense as a share of all federal outlays |
| 1950 | 15.6% | 32% |
| 1960 | 17.8% | 52% |
| 1970 | 19.3% | 42% |
| 1980 | 21.7% | 23% |

stem: Taken together, the table best supports which conclusion about the federal government from 1950 to 1980?

options.text: It grew because defense spending took a larger share of the budget every decade.
options.misconception: The defense share falls after 1960, from 52 percent to 23 percent.

options.text: Its size and its main job both stayed the same across all thirty years.
options.misconception: Both columns change at every step, so neither size nor mix stayed the same.

options.text: It grew smaller overall while spending more and more money on defense each year.
options.misconception: The first column rises and the defense share falls, the opposite of this claim.

options.text: It kept growing, but what it spent most on shifted from defense toward domestic programs.

rationales.A: The defense share falls after 1960, from 52 percent to 23 percent.
rationales.B: Both columns change at every step, so neither size nor mix stayed the same.
rationales.C: The first column rises and the defense share falls, the opposite of this claim.
rationales.D: The first column rises at every step while the defense share falls from 52 percent in 1960 to 23 percent in 1980.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the first column's start and end: 15.6 percent in 1950, 21.7 percent in 1980, rising at every step.
2. Compare the second column's peak and end: 52 percent in 1960, 23 percent in 1980.
3. A bigger total with a smaller defense share means domestic spending filled the difference.
4. Background: The shift matches the growth of Social Security, Medicare, and other domestic programs in the 1960s and 1970s.
Remember: A table's story is in how its columns move together, not in one row alone.
